title: Weekly Research Brief: Anthropic IPO, ‘MEV Bros’ Acquittal, Solana Breakpoint
summary: This week, Alex Thorn breaks down the market ramifications of Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO; Thad Pinakiewicz examines the acquittal of the “MEV brothers”; and Lucas Tcheyan shares takeaways from Solana’s annual Breakpoint confab.

Welcome to Galaxy Research's Weekly Research Brief.[Subscribe](https://www.galaxy.com/subscribe-to-research?utm_campaign=Weekly%20Research%20Brief%20-%20Email&utm_medium=email&utm_source=hs_email&_hsenc=p2ANqtz--YWOkviRZJsa_uYNPjl2N4ahqTpHeV86Rs9VQQeL9MWn1U09L_xNxjRhoRyGaaBrCPLXuX) to get this newsletter delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.


This week, Alex Thorn breaks down the market ramifications of Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO; Thad Pinakiewicz explains the acquittal of the “MEV brothers”; and Lucas Tcheyan shares takeaways from Solana’s annual Breakpoint confab.


## Anthropic Prices Record IPO in a Market – and World – on Edge


#### WHAT HAPPENED


**Anthropic**[completed](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/18/anthropic-ipo-ai-offering-price.html) **the largest IPO in history on Wednesday evening, pricing at $83 per share, after updating its prospectus last week with an expected price range of $70 to $78.** Strong demand led the AI company, best known for its Claude chatbot, to upsize its offering, selling about 980 million shares and raising $81.3 billion, up from the 825 million originally planned. That figure surpasses Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June, and Anthropic's IPO price implied a valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion for a company founded barely six years ago. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led the deal, as they did for SpaceX. Ahead of the open, Cboe’s JJ Kinahan[said](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/anthropic-opens-today-demand-seven-175239862.html) demand was running almost seven times the offering, and CNBC sources reported that retail demand was the largest in history.


Shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT at 11:48 a.m. ET on Thursday. The first print was $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, which briefly gave the company a market capitalization of $2 trillion. The stock hit its intraday high of $114.99 in the minute after the first trade and then spent the rest of the session fading. By the afternoon it was trading in the mid-$90s, at $94.67, up about 14% from the offering price, as of 2:18 p.m. ET. The decline from the open was unusually steep. Of 20 big US IPOs since 2008, only Coupang was doing worse at the same point in its first day, according to Yahoo Finance; the group’s average was up about 3.5%. The broader market also sold off as soon as the stock opened. Stocks fell to their session lows the moment Anthropic began trading, and chip stocks including Nvidia and Broadcom erased their gains. Listed ANT options are set to start trading on Monday.


Onchain, Hyperliquid showed the success of its[pre-IPO perp market](https://www.galaxy.com/insights/research/weekly-top-stories-05-22-26-ethereum-foundation-exits-pre-ipo-crypto-markets-fed-payment-rails) yet again. Its markets correctly called the deal pricing, with the perp trading well above the $70-78 range for weeks, signaling that demand was stronger than the underwriters’ original target. The perp ultimately undershot the open by about 7%, with the contract trading around $103.67 at 8:40 AM ET, roughly 25% above the $83/share offer price. Thursday morning’s perp price was roughly in line with market consensus (Cboe’s Kinahan[said](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/anthropic-opens-today-demand-seven-175239862.html) the first trade should land around $103 or $104), but ultimately both the perps and the pros were off with the first trade ultimately printing at $111.50.


But the perp nailed where the stock ended up trading. For most of the week before listing, the perp sat in the mid-to-high $90s. It was about $96.93 as of Nov. 17 and $98.83 on the hourly chart the night before pricing, having briefly fallen below $94 during the earlier tech selloff. After the opening pop faded, the stock traded right back into that band, around $94–$97 by the afternoon. One could argue the perp’s week-long equilibrium was a better estimate of “fair” first-day value than the opening print, which looked like a short-lived demand spike.


**OUR TAKE**


There was something strange about watching Anthropic’s staff clap on the Nasdaq floor as they IPO’d a company whose primary media narrative is that AI might kill us all.


This week has been the most *doomer* week in recent memory, coming off the back of Microsoft’s O365 outage Thursday, the nationwide FAA ground stop Friday, bank outages on Monday, even the NSA’s internal comms system reportedly disrupted (twice?). Costco[reported](https://money.usnews.com/investing/news/articles/2026-11-17/costco-sees-demand-lift-from-outage-driven-stockpiling-mizuho-says) a wave of panic buying, people[pulled cash](https://cnbc.com/2026/11/19/banking-outages-emergency-cash.html) out of banks, and[prepping](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/wave-outages-americans-preparing-doomsday-121328549.html) content[went viral](https://en.tengrinews.kz/kazakhstan_news/stock-up-on-food-before-november-17-why-the-entire-internet-274610/) on social media. Chatter among traders included tips on which types of solar-powered batteries to buy, how to store substantial amounts of dry food in a New York City apartment, and which are the best routes to escape the city in the event of a grid collapse. So maybe it’s only fitting that this week’s blockbuster IPO was one in which the S-1’s risk factors[included](https://www.fortune.com/2026/10/26/anthropic-s1-risk-factors-existential-risk-pentagon-dario-amodei/) “the end of humanity.” (Although we are not equity analysts, we agree that the end of humanity *could* materially affect Anthropic’s earnings.)


Since Oct. 1, the S&P 500 is down 7%, gold is off 12.2%, and BTC is in the red 25%. Treasuries have depreciated, inflation is hot, rates are expected to rise, commodities are falling, and the Democrats swept to power largely on calls to solve the “affordability crisis.” Our own Bitcoin fear & greed index is printing near all-time lows (meaning “extreme fear”), the VIX is trading at levels comparable to those from the breakout of the Iran War in March, though not quite the level from the “Tariff Tantrum” in April 2025. Stanley Druckenmiller[said](https://x.com/TheTranscript_/status/2123163288196600167) he is “more uncertain than ever after 50 years of investing” and that his firm’s equity positions are “basically flat.” Another Wall Street luminary, Howard Marks,[argued](https://newsable.asianetnews.com/markets/howard-marks-calls-ai-exposure-a-fault-line-running-through-portfolios-highlights-nearly-600b-in-ai-related-debt-issuance-articleshow-gzqtd48) in a Nov. 11[memo](https://eu.36kr.com/en/p/4066318718423941) entitled “A Layman Thinks About AI” that the breakneck speed of AI development is a big risk, even for Anthropic. Paul Tudor Jones[said](https://alpha-maven.com/story/hedge-fund/billionaire-paul-tudor-jones-has-message-for-stock-market-investors-tradingview) in mid-October that “2027 is going to be a really difficult year for the stock market.” So it’s fair to say the stock market intelligentsia is uneasy.


Some have theorized that recent risk asset headwinds were enhanced by the liquidity drain caused by allocators pulling assets to buy the Anthropic IPO. This does feel intuitively right, though there’s not much evidence to directly support it. Bitcoin’s price did behave similarly when it traded poorly into the SpaceX IPO in June and made its current bear-market low on July 1 ($57,717 on Coinbase). Whether BTC and other risk assets will receive some respite now that ANT is a public stock remains to be seen.


The reality is that Americans are fearful and psychologically traumatized. Polarization has long been a characteristic of the American political landscape, but the Democratic sweep was so dramatic that big swings are expected on things like tax policy, AI policy, legislative priorities, and more. Layer on the never-ending drumbeat of cyber vulnerabilities and a spectrum of AI outcomes that is so wide it contains both the possibilities of permanent utopia and impending obliteration of the species, and it’s easy to see why markets are unsteady. There’s a sense that one more piece of big bad news could tip markets over the edge – a major cyber-attack, an escalation of the Iran or Ukraine wars, an outbreak or substantial natural disaster. Alternatively, a major peace deal or initiative emanating from Trump’s visit with Xi and Putin, cessation of major regional conflicts, or a legislative breakthrough in Congress could assuage the fears.


As they say, if you’re going through hell, keep going.[The only way out is through](https://thepoetryhour.com/poems/a-servant-to-servants/) . Everything is different, yes, but[everything is fine](https://www.galaxy.com/insights/podcasts/galaxy-brains/midterms-and-markets-with-tyler-williams) . Bitcoin keeps[producing blocks uninterrupted](https://mempool.space/) , and I just coded a slick new dashboard to monitor the situation.[– Alex Thorn](https://x.com/intangiblecoins)


## Who Sandwiches the Sandwichers? ‘MEV Bros’ Acquitted on Fraud Charges


#### WHAT HAPPENED


**On Nov. 16, Judge Jessica Clarke**[acquitted](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/akvewgjxkvr/11162026peraire.pdf) **Anton and James Peraire-Bueno of wire fraud and related charges, ending the first criminal case built around MEV, the profit available to whoever decides the order of transactions on a blockchain** .


In practice, that “whoever” means validators and the builders to whom they outsource. A whole industry of bots exists to pay them for favorable placement. The brothers set a trap for some of those bots, ones whose own business is jumping in front of other people’s trades, which makes for an unusual set of victims. Using a flaw in Ethereum’s block-building software, the pair saw what those bots were about to do, something the system was designed to prevent, and turned it against them. The brothers walked away with about $25 million in roughly twelve seconds, at the cost of a protocol penalty of about 1 ETH (worth ~$3,000 at the time).


#### OUR TAKE


The judge did not say any of this was fine. She said wire fraud requires a lie, and the government never showed that the brothers told one. This relatively narrow ruling leaves a lot unresolved. Below, we walk through what the court found, then the questions it raises about manipulation law, sandwich trading, validator obligations, and whether code really is law.


##### What the Court Found


Some background first, because this is not a simple case to wrap your head around. Validators are the participants chosen to propose new blocks on Ethereum. Most of them hand off the work of assembling those blocks to specialized builders, through intermediaries called[relays](https://docs.flashbots.net/flashbots-mev-boost/introduction) . A relay keeps a block’s contents hidden from the network until the validator signs off on it. The targets here were sandwich bots, which buy just ahead of someone else’s pending trade and sell right after it. The brothers baited those bots with transactions built to look like ideal sandwich targets. The brothers’ own validator then signed off on a block with deliberately bogus fields. The relay checked that the signature was valid, but not those fields, and revealed the block’s contents. The brothers rebuilt the block, kept the bots’ purchases, and swapped out the bait for transactions that sold the same tokens into the prices the bots had just pushed up, leaving the bots holding the bag. Their validator was[slashed](https://ethereum.org/developers/docs/consensus-mechanisms/pos/rewards-and-penalties/) about 1 ETH for the misdeed of[proposing two blocks for one slot](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/akvewgjxkvr/11162026peraire.pdf#page=16) .


The government outlined what it thought were two lies, and the court rejected both. The first alleged lie was the bait transaction. The court found no evidence that placing a transaction in the mempool, Ethereum’s public waiting room,[conveys an agreement to be sandwiched](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/akvewgjxkvr/11162026peraire.pdf#page=28) . Nor does a transaction promise to be part of anyone’s bundle, or to land in any particular spot in a block, or any given block at all. Exploiting another market participant's expectations, even intentionally and profitably, doesn’t necessarily amount to a lie. The court[drew that point](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/akvewgjxkvr/11162026peraire.pdf#page=29) from the Mango Markets case,[United States v. Eisenberg](https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2025-05/23cr10%20Opinion%20and%20Order.pdf) . Avi Eisenberg pumped the price of Mango’s token and borrowed[over $100 million](https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2025-05/23cr10%20Opinion%20and%20Order.pdf#page=3) against his inflated position. Mango had[no terms of service](https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2025-05/23cr10%20Opinion%20and%20Order.pdf#page=30) , and the court found that Eisenberg’s borrowing made no promises, explicit or implicit.


The second alleged lie was the signature on the bogus block. The government argued that by signing a block header with fields they knew were invalid, the brothers made a false statement to the relay. The court rejected the theory on two fronts. First, a validator’s signature is a[commitment to publish the block or accept slashing](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/akvewgjxkvr/11162026peraire.pdf#page=37) , not a promise of anything else. Ethereum, and trustless blockchains more broadly, are systems where everyone expects validators to act in[“their own rational self-interest—whatever that is.”](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/akvewgjxkvr/11162026peraire.pdf#page=32) Registering a validator with a MEV-Boost relay[doesn’t come with any terms of use](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/akvewgjxkvr/11162026peraire.pdf#page=8) . Second,[the relay wasn’t checking those fields at all](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/akvewgjxkvr/11162026peraire.pdf#page=39) . It would have revealed the block’s contents no matter what the brothers put there. The same bug that made the exploit possible also made the “lie” immaterial.


##### Was Wire Fraud the Wrong Charge?


Wire fraud requires deception. The[Commodity Exchange Act](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/7/9) , by contrast, separately prohibits manipulative trading and deceptive devices, so an artificial-price scheme can violate it without anyone telling a lie. Eisenberg’s wire fraud conviction[fell for lack of a false representation](https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2025-05/23cr10%20Opinion%20and%20Order.pdf#page=29) , but his commodities fraud and manipulation convictions were vacated only because prosecutors brought them in the[wrong venue](https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2025-05/23cr10%20Opinion%20and%20Order.pdf#page=3) , and the judge[found the evidence on those counts sufficient](https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2025-05/23cr10%20Opinion%20and%20Order.pdf#page=21) . Judge Clarke, of the U.S. Court of the Southern District of New York, was similarly careful. She framed the question as whether the evidence supported wire fraud, not whether the brothers’ conduct was right, moral, or a violation of[“uncharged crimes.”](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/akvewgjxkvr/11162026peraire.pdf#page=1) Neither ruling is a safe harbor for DeFi manipulation.


##### Are Sandwich Attacks Legal?


If manipulating prices through transaction ordering can violate the Commodity Exchange Act, sandwich trading itself starts to look exposed. The court observed that[“no trader ... would agree to be sandwiched,”](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/akvewgjxkvr/11162026peraire.pdf#page=28) but it never decided whether the bots’ own strategy was lawful. The CFTC[retains](https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2026-05-29_R48963_3e79ce8e188e8f277bc29ccdd3a067ef92eacf68.html) antifraud and anti-manipulation authority over spot commodity markets, digital commodities included.


##### Slashing Is a Price, Not a Prohibition


The validator half of the case raises a design problem more than a legal one. By reading the brothers’ signature as a commitment to publish a block or be slashed, the court treated slashing as a price rather than a prohibition. Ethereum’s guarantees hold only as long as deviating from expected behavior costs more than it pays, and here a 1 ETH penalty stood against a $25 million payoff.


##### Code Is Law?


Sort of. The Eisenberg case and the MEV brothers ruling both refuse to turn a developer’s intentions into binding promises without evidence. Terms and conditions could become the standard for protocols looking for legal recourse in the future, but a frontend popup gating access may not bind someone interacting directly with smart contracts. Following the code doesn’t protect you from anti-manipulation statutes either. The court rejected the idea that[“undermining the spirit of a system alone constitutes fraud.”](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/akvewgjxkvr/11162026peraire.pdf#page=40) What it does say is that, for wire fraud purposes, expectations alone don’t create a promise, and absent an actual agreement, the code is the closest thing to one.


Code isn’t law, but it is the closest thing to a contract you get when nobody signs anything else. The brothers read that contract more carefully than anyone on Ethereum, including the people who wrote the relay. If your protocol’s security depends on validators not doing the math on a 1 ETH penalty against a $25 million payoff, you don’t have a security model. **–**[Thad Pinakiewicz](https://x.com/thethadp)


## Solana’s Institutional Breakpoint


**Solana's annual**[Breakpoint conference](https://solana.com/news/day-1-at-breakpoint-2026-mainnet-1-0-zelle-and-londons-crypto-moment) **took place Nov. 15–17 in London under the theme "Token Supercycle," showcasing the network's growing ambitions in payments, tokenization, and institutional finance.**


The event also marked Solana's graduation from "mainnet beta" to Mainnet 1.0, following a series of infrastructure upgrades that halved target block times to 200 milliseconds (ms) and reduced target finality to approximately 150 ms through the[Alpenglow consensus protocol](https://solana.com/uk/upgrades/alpenglow) .


Institutional adoption dominated the announcements. Zelle, the bank-owned payments network that[processed more than $1.2 trillion in 2025](https://www.zelle.com/press-releases/zelle-posts-20-growth-12-trillion-sent-far-outpacing-consumer-spending-and-cementing) , demonstrated a $1.25 million confidential stablecoin transfer and outlined plans to launch ZelleUSD on Solana for international payments. Global remittance giant MoneyGram and wallet provider Solflare announced USDC-to-cash conversions across 170 countries and territories, while fintech lender SoFi highlighted Solana as a preferred network for stablecoins and tokenized assets.


Tokenization was another major theme. The[DTCC outlined plans](https://www.dtcc.com/press-releases/2026/dtcc-tokenization-service-to-connect-with-solana) to connect its Tokenization Service to Solana in the second half of 2027, while wealth management platform[Allfunds](https://solana.com/news/project-harmonia-brings-institutional-tokenized-funds-to-solana) , banking giant BNY, and investment manager Baillie Gifford highlighted initiatives bringing traditional investment products onchain. Other announcements spanned tokenized equities, regulated derivatives, decentralized compute, and agentic payments, reflecting Solana's efforts to expand beyond its established strengths in retail trading and decentralized finance.


#### OUR TAKE


Solana's evolution since 2023 has created a growing disconnect between how the network is perceived and what its ecosystem is attempting to become.


For less engaged observers, Solana remains synonymous with memecoin speculation and the sometimes unsavory activity that accompanies it. For those following the ecosystem more closely, however, the network is increasingly positioning itself as infrastructure for payments, tokenized assets, and other forms of financial activity that could bring considerably larger pools of users and capital onchain.


These two identities are not mutually exclusive. Solana's success as an onchain casino has been a powerful engine for attracting users, developers, liquidity, and investment. Its ability to support high-frequency, low-value financial transactions at scale helped establish a competitive advantage in a market where speed, cost, and usability were often sufficient to win. However, the conditions that allowed Solana to dominate that segment are materially different from those governing the next phase of adoption. Payments, tokenization, and agentic commerce are increasingly attracting the attention of the world's largest financial institutions, payment providers, and technology companies. These players have considerably greater resources and distribution than crypto-native startups, and Solana is one of several networks they are exploring, alongside proprietary infrastructure they can develop and control themselves.


For institutions, performance is increasingly a prerequisite rather than a differentiator. Privacy, compliance, operational accountability, distribution, and access to pools of liquidity are equally consequential. Solana's realistic opportunity, at least in the near term, is therefore less about becoming the universal settlement layer for global finance and more about establishing itself as a leading neutral venue for the subset of financial activity that benefits from shared, composable, high-performance public infrastructure.


A[recent paper from J.P. Morgan's Kinexys and MIT's Digital Currency Initiative](https://www.jpmorgan.com/payments/newsroom/kinexys-mit-dci-institutional-open-blockchain) illustrates the challenge. Financial institutions recognize the appeal of public blockchains as shared infrastructure that no single participant controls, the paper notes. But their requirements for confidentiality, compliance, governance, and other operational necessities can conflict with the characteristics that make these networks valuable in the first place. Accommodating those requirements often means reintroducing intermediaries, permissioning, or centralized controls, potentially undermining the neutrality and interoperability that distinguish public blockchains from traditional systems. Yet building proprietary networks creates its own challenges, particularly when competing institutions must coordinate across fragmented systems. The likely outcome is not a wholesale migration from private to public infrastructure, but a gradual and selective adoption of public networks where their advantages are sufficiently compelling.


Breakpoint offered evidence of the opportunity and its limitations. Zelle's confidential-transfer demonstration, DTCC's planned integration, and initiatives from major asset managers suggest that Solana is increasingly being considered for financial activity well beyond its crypto-native base. Its presence in tokenized-equity trading also demonstrates that the network can attract meaningful activity in emerging asset classes. Solana[accounted](https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/static.bitwiseinvestments.com/Research/bitwise-tokenization-247-trading-and-the-economics-of-solana-2026.pdf) for approximately 42% of onchain tokenized-equity trading volume between January and September 2026. But there is an important distinction between being selected as a supported network and becoming the primary venue where liquidity, users, and economic activity ultimately concentrate. DTCC's integration, for example, forms part of a broader multichain strategy rather than an exclusive commitment to Solana.


Nor is Solana entering these markets without crypto-native competition. Hyperliquid remains a formidable competitor in onchain perpetual derivatives, while the[emerging agentic economy](https://www.galaxy.com/insights/research/x402-ai-agents-crypto-payments) has yet to produce a clear winner or a compelling reason why payment and coordination infrastructure must concentrate on Solana. Privacy tooling is improving, but its maturity, regulatory compatibility, and institutional adoption remain important questions. These dynamics make the ecosystem's ability to attract and retain builders particularly consequential. Solana's dense developer culture and willingness to experiment have been central to its recovery and growth, and preserving those characteristics will matter as the network courts institutional capital.


Solana has made substantial progress in addressing the technical limitations that once threatened its credibility. The more difficult task ahead is translating that progress into durable distribution, liquidity, and institutional dependence in markets where performance alone is unlikely to determine the winner.


Breakpoint demonstrated that Solana has earned a place in those conversations. Whether it can turn that position into an enduring advantage, rather than remain one capable option in an increasingly competitive and multichain financial system, is the more consequential question. -[Lucas Tcheyan](https://x.com/Uptodatenow)

## Chart of the Week: Back Up the Wagon


Among the investment managers that file quarterly 13-F reports with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Wells Fargo is now the largest holder of spot bitcoin exchange-traded products (ETPs).


As of Sept. 30, the financial services giant held the equivalent of 30,553 BTC, worth $2.55 billion, across 10 funds. That’s up from 15,931 on June 30. Wells passed trading firm Jane Street (23,167), previously the largest holder.


The 15 largest holders are a cross-section of the institutional market: wealth platforms, market makers, bank trading desks, hedge funds, asset managers, one sovereign wealth fund, and one crypto investment firm.


That mix matters for interpretation. The same number of shares can be a client’s allocation at a wealth platform, inventory at a market maker, or one leg of a hedged trade at a hedge fund.


In the case of Wells Fargo, 85% of its filed holdings sit in its advisor or broker-dealer entities, suggestive of client holdings rather than principal bank positions.


For more insights, read our recent[analysis](https://www.galaxy.com/insights/research/bitcoin-etp-13f-institutional-holdings-q3-2026-wealth-channel-wells-fargo) of the Q3 13-F filings and follow[@glxyresearch](https://x.com/glxyresearch) on X. –[Alex Thorn](https://x.com/intangiblecoins)
